check.q: A line of fit for car age (years) and price (thousands of dollars) has slope −2. What does it mean?
choices: Each extra year adds $2,000 to the price.
Each extra year of age goes with about $2,000 less in price.
check.why: Slope is the change in price per year. Negative means price falls, and the unit is thousands of dollars.

lessons.title: Intercept and Predictions
lessons.mainIdea: The y-intercept is the line's value when the horizontal variable is 0; it means something only if 0 is inside or near the data.
reading: In the line score = 5 × hours + 43, set hours to 0 and the score is 43. That number is the *y-intercept*, where the line crosses the vertical axis. Does it mean a student with no sleep would score 43? No. No student in the data slept 0 hours; the least was 5. The intercept here is a mathematical anchor, not a fact about zero-sleep students.

Sometimes the intercept does mean something. A line for taxi fares, fare = 2.5 × miles + 3, has intercept 3. At 0 miles the fare is $3, which is the flat fee for getting in the cab. Here 0 miles is a real starting point. To predict, plug in: 8 miles gives 2.5 × 8 + 3 = 20 + 3 = 23 dollars. A line with slope −2 and intercept 50, y = −2x + 50, gives y = −2 × 15 + 50 = −30 + 50 = 20 when x = 15.

Always ask two questions about a prediction. Is the input inside the *range of the data*? Does the answer make sense? A line for ice cream sales, cones = 4 × temp − 100, predicts 4 × 80 − 100 = 220 cones at 80°F, which is sensible. At 20°F it predicts 4 × 20 − 100 = −20 cones, which is impossible; that temperature is far outside the summer data. Common mistake: reading the intercept as "the starting value" in every situation.

words.d: the value of the line where the horizontal variable is 0
the stretch from the smallest to the largest measured input; predictions are safest inside it

look.title: Taxi Fare Line
look.text: A line of fit for cab rides in a city is fare = 2.5 × miles + 3, with fare in dollars and distance in miles.
look.prompt: What does the intercept 3 mean here? What fare does the line predict for a 6-mile ride, and for a 12-mile ride?

check.q: Using y = 2.5x + 10, what is y when x = 8?
A line has slope −2 and y-intercept 50. What is y when x = 15?
check.why: −2 × 15 = −30, and −30 + 50 = 20. Adding 30 instead gives 80.

check.q: For the taxi line fare = 2.5 × miles + 3, what does the intercept 3 mean?
choices: A ride costs $3 before any miles are driven, like a flat fee.
The intercept has no meaning here.
check.why: At 0 miles the fare is 2.5 × 0 + 3 = 3. Zero miles is a real starting point, so the intercept is the base charge.

lessons.title: Two-Way Tables
lessons.mainIdea: A two-way table counts people by two categories at once; row and column totals let you check the count and answer how-many questions.
reading: Some data are categories, not numbers: grade level, cat or dog, yes or no. This is *categorical data*. A *two-way table* organizes counts by two categories at once. Survey 100 students: do you prefer cats or dogs? Rows are grade (7th, 8th), columns are the pet. Seventh grade: 20 cats, 30 dogs. Eighth grade: 15 cats, 35 dogs. Add each row: 7th total 50, 8th total 50. Add each column: cats 35, dogs 65. The grand total is 100 either way, which confirms the table.

Each *cell* answers one how-many question. How many eighth graders prefer dogs? 35. How many students prefer cats? Read the column total: 35. How many seventh graders were surveyed? Read the row total: 50. Given some cells, you can find missing ones by subtraction. If 80 students are surveyed, 50 play a sport, and 18 of those also play an instrument, then 50 − 18 = 32 play a sport but no instrument.

Common mistakes: mixing up row and column when reading a cell, and double-counting when categories overlap. Each person belongs in exactly one cell. Also, do not use a two-way table when a variable is numerical, like exact height; use a scatter plot for two numerical variables. Two categories, two-way table; two numbers, scatter plot.

words.d: data sorted into groups with names, like yes/no or cat/dog, instead of numbers
a table that counts how many fall into each pair of categories
one box in the table, holding the count for one pair of categories

look.title: Pet Preference by Grade (100 students)
look.cite: Class survey used in this lesson (made-up example)
look.prompt: Find the row totals, the column totals and the grand total. How many students prefer dogs?

check.q: In the pet table, how many students in all prefer cats?
check.why: Add the cat column: 20 + 15 = 35. The dog column adds to 65.

check.q: 80 students are surveyed: 50 play a sport, and 18 of those also play an instrument. How many play a sport but no instrument?
Which pair of variables belongs in a two-way table?
choices: hours of sleep and quiz score
check.why: Both are categories. The other pairs are two numerical measurements, which belong on a scatter plot.

lessons.title: Relative Frequencies
lessons.mainIdea: Divide a cell by its row total (or column total) to get a relative frequency, which lets you compare groups of different sizes.
reading: Counts alone can mislead when groups differ in size. Use *relative frequency*: a count divided by a total. In the pet table, 30 of the 50 seventh graders prefer dogs: 30/50 = 0.6, or 60%. For eighth graders, 35/50 = 0.7, or 70%. Dividing by the *row total* gives row relative frequencies. Because both grades had 50 students, the counts and the percents tell the same story here.

Now a table with unequal groups. 80 students: 50 play a sport and 30 do not. Of the sport players, 18 play an instrument. Of the non-players, 12 do. Raw counts, 18 versus 12, make it look like sport players play instruments more. But 18/50 = 0.36, or 36%, and 12/30 = 0.4, or 40%. The non-players actually have the higher share. Compare percents, not counts, when the groups are different sizes.

You can also divide by the grand total to get the share of everyone: 18/80 = 0.225, so 22.5% of all students play both a sport and an instrument. Choose the total that matches the question. "What percent of sport players" means divide by the sport row. "What percent of all students" means divide by 80. Common mistake: dividing by the wrong total, or mixing a row percent with a column percent in one comparison.

words.d: a count divided by a total, written as a fraction, decimal or percent
the sum of all the cells in one row of the table

look.title: Sport and Instrument (80 students)
look.cite: Class survey used in this lesson (made-up example)
look.prompt: What percent of sport players play an instrument? What percent of non-players do? Which group has the higher share?

check.q: Of 50 sport players, 18 play an instrument. What is the row relative frequency?
check.why: 18 ÷ 50 = 0.36, or 36%. Dividing by 80 gives 22.5%, the share of all students.

check.q: 12 of the 30 non-players play an instrument. What percent is that?
Why compare relative frequencies instead of counts?
choices: Groups of different sizes can be compared fairly as percents.
Percents are always larger than counts.
Relative frequencies do not need totals.
check.why: A percent puts each group on the same scale, so 18 of 50 and 12 of 30 can be compared directly.

lessons.title: Association in a Table
lessons.mainIdea: Two categories are associated when the row percents differ noticeably between rows; similar percents mean little or no association.
reading: Is there an association between playing a sport and playing an instrument? Compare the row percents: 36% of sport players play an instrument, and 40% of non-players do. Those are close, only 4 *percentage points* apart. Knowing whether a student plays a sport tells you little about instruments. That is weak or no association.

Now a different survey of 200 students: studied with a group or alone, and passed or did not. Group: 60 passed, 20 did not, total 80. Alone: 60 passed, 60 did not, total 120. Row percents: group 60/80 = 0.75, or 75% passed. Alone 60/120 = 0.5, or 50% passed. Notice the raw pass counts are the same, 60 and 60, but the percents differ by 25 percentage points. That is a clear *association*: students who studied in groups passed at a higher rate.

Association again is not proof of cause. Group studiers might already be stronger students. Also, a difference of a couple of percentage points in small groups is not convincing; 5 of 10 versus 6 of 10 is one student. Common mistakes: comparing counts across rows of different size, and comparing a row percent to a column percent. Pick one direction, compute both rows, then compare.

words.d: in a table, a difference in the row percents that shows the two categories are linked
the difference between two percents, like 75% minus 50% = 25 percentage points

look.prompt: Compute the percent passing in each row. Is there an association? Does it prove that group study causes passing?

check.q: Group: 60 of 80 passed. Alone: 60 of 120 passed. What percent of each group passed?
check.why: 60 ÷ 80 = 0.75 and 60 ÷ 120 = 0.5. The counts match, but the percents do not.

check.q: Two row percents are 36% and 40%. What does this suggest?
choices: the second row caused the first
little or no association between the two categories
check.why: A gap of 4 percentage points is small, so knowing the row tells you little about the column.

check.q: Which is the fairest way to look for an association in a two-way table?
choices: Compare the raw counts in one column.
Compare a row percent to a column percent.
Compare the grand total to one cell.
Compare the percent in each row that falls in the same column.
check.why: Row percents put rows of different sizes on the same scale, so a difference between them shows a real link.

review.q: Points on a scatter plot fall from upper left to lower right. Which association is this?
review.why: One variable decreases as the other increases, so the trend is negative.

review.q: What is the slope of a line through (2, 10) and (6, 22)?
Using y = 3x + 5, what is y when x = 10?
A point sits far from a rising band of points. What is it called?
review.why: A point that does not follow the pattern the others follow is an outlier.

review.q: In a two-way table of 100 students, 35 prefer cats and the rest prefer dogs. How many prefer dogs?
24 of 40 seventh graders bring lunch; 30 of 60 eighth graders do. Which grade has the higher share?
review.why: 24 ÷ 40 = 0.6 and 30 ÷ 60 = 0.5. Counts mislead because the groups differ in size.

review.q: What is the y-intercept of y = −2x + 50?
A line of fit was made from students who slept 5 to 9 hours. Why not use it to predict a score for 20 hours?
choices: Lines can only predict values under 10.
20 hours is far outside the range of the data, so the line may not apply.
review.why: A line of fit is only supported where there are data. Far outside that range it can give impossible values.
